input:
Principle
Distillation is a separation process in which a liquid mixture is separated into fractions of differing composition by boiling and condensation. The underlying principle is a difference in volatility between the components. When a liquid mixture boils, the vapour formed is richer in the more volatile components than the liquid from which it arises, since the more volatile components pass into the vapour more readily at the boiling temperature. If this vapour is condensed, the resulting liquid has the composition of the vapour, and if it is boiled again, a further enrichment takes place. A single step of boiling and condensation changes the composition only to a limited extent, so in practice the step is repeated many times within a column, in which vapour and liquid are brought into contact on each stage.
In the simple model used to describe the process, each stage is treated as an equilibrium stage: the vapour and the liquid leaving a stage are assumed to be in equilibrium with each other, so their compositions are determined by the equilibrium relationship for the mixture at the temperature and pressure of the stage. The relative volatility, which expresses the comparison between the two components' proportions in the vapour and in the liquid, measures how far the composition is moved by a single equilibrium contact. Where relative volatility is close to unity, the vapour and liquid compositions are nearly the same, and separation proceeds only slowly. A further feature is reflux, in which part of the condensed vapour is returned to the column as liquid, so the rising vapour meets liquid richer in the less volatile component as it ascends, and the enrichment builds up from stage to stage rather than being used up in a single contact.
Equipment
The column is a vertical shell in which vapour rises and liquid flows down. Contact between the phases is brought about either by trays, horizontal plates holding a layer of liquid through which the vapour bubbles, or by packing, a bed of small pieces presenting a large surface over which the liquid spreads as a film. Whether trays or packing are used depends on the duty, including the pressure drop across the bed, the tendency of the liquid to foul the surfaces, and the ease with which the internals can be cleaned and inspected.
Heat is supplied at the base by a reboiler, which boils part of the liquid leaving the bottom of the column and returns the vapour to the shell. At the top, a condenser condenses the vapour leaving the column; part of the condensate is drawn off as distillate and the remainder is returned as reflux. The feed is introduced at an intermediate level, at the stage whose composition most closely matches the feed. The liquid leaving the base, depleted in the more volatile component, is drawn off as bottoms. Instruments on the column record temperatures along its height, and a temperature change at a level indicates that the composition held there has changed.
Worked example
Consider a feed of two components, the more volatile denoted A and the other B, and let the mole fraction of A in the feed be denoted by $z$, in the distillate by $x_D$ and in the bottoms by $x_B$. The example sets out what the simple model requires for a separation that yields a distillate rich in A together with a bottoms poor in A, drawing only on the relationships established in the principle part.
An overall material balance shows that the molar flow of the feed is equal to the molar flow of the distillate plus the molar flow of the bottoms. A component balance on A likewise shows that the amount of A in the feed is equal to the sum of the amounts of A in the two products. Together, the two balances determine the split between distillate and bottoms once the three compositions have been selected: a distillate composition close to the feed composition calls for a large distillate flow, and a sharp separation, in which $x_D$ approaches the pure component and $x_B$ approaches zero, is possible only where the balances leave a positive flow for each product.
Within the column, the composition changes from stage to stage. The vapour rising from a stage carries the equilibrium composition corresponding to the liquid held on that stage, while the liquid flowing downwards carries the composition of the stage it is leaving. Stepping through the column from the condenser downwards, the vapour of each stage is richer in A than the vapour of the stage beneath it, since each contact moves the composition toward A by the amount the equilibrium relationship permits. The balances serve as a check on the stepping: the compositions at the two ends of the column must, when the products are recombined in the proportions the balances give, reproduce the feed. The outcome of the example is a statement of feasibility. Where the balances admit the chosen compositions and the equilibrium relationship moves the composition at every stage, the separation can be staged; the number of stages the movement calls for is governed by how far the composition is moved at each stage, which the equilibrium relationship alone determines.
Limits
The simple model breaks down where the assumptions on which it rests no longer hold. The relative volatility is treated as constant, whereas in a real mixture it varies with composition and temperature, and it may approach unity over part of the range; where this happens, the movement of composition at each stage shrinks, and the staging argument of the worked example understates what the separation requires. Certain mixtures form an azeotrope, a composition at which the vapour and the liquid have the same composition; at such a composition an equilibrium contact moves nothing, and ordinary distillation cannot carry a separation beyond that point.
The equilibrium-stage assumption also fails in practice. The vapour and the liquid on an actual tray leave the tray before equilibrium between them has been reached, because contact time and mixing are both limited, so a real stage moves the composition by less than the model suggests. The model also leaves out the pressure drop along the column and the heat exchanged with the surroundings, both of which shift the temperatures at which the stages operate. The model is therefore a framework for reasoning about the separation — balances, equilibrium and staging — rather than a means of predicting the compositions a particular column will deliver.

When a liquid mixture boils, the vapour formed is richer in the more volatile components than the liquid from which it forms, because the more volatile components pass into the vapour more readily at the boiling temperature.
